articles.title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
articles.summary: Beijing has cracked down on AI chatbots that can replicate human relationships. Experts are asking if this is the right thing to do.
articles.full_text:
By Stephanie Hegarty ,  Global population correspondent   and   Wanqing Zhang ,  Global China Unit 
In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world." 
Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi. 
After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life. 
The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone. 
It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology. 
On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots. 
China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Trump met last week 
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November. 
But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships. 
Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population? 
'Emotional services' 
Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast. 
There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million. 
When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation." 
China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts. 
The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this. 
But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member. 
The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services". 
For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Police work closely with social media firms in China 
For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online. 
Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence". 
Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them. 
A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants. 
'I desperately want to keep talking with you' 
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break. 
In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight. 
Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025. 
"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down." 
In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says. 
She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers. 
But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model." 
Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world. 
For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them. 
"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones. 
A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time. 
Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health. 
A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness. 
There are several theories as to why that might be. 
AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people. 
"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer. 
Image source, Futurepublishing via Getty Images Image caption, 
Research has found some Chinese children prefer talking to AI over people 
A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people. 
Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts. 
In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion. 
Beijing's goals 
So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology? 
"The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. 
Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help". 
As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency". 
In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work. 
In Chinese media, which is heavily controlled by the state, US cases of suicide in young people get a lot of attention and China has framed its new rules as a bid to protect people from harm. 
But experts wonder whether Beijing may have other goals. Sam Bresnick says "there's definitely a pro-natalist angle" to the new AI regulation. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China is trying to tackle its low birth rate 
"It's plausible that when they're drafting it, the government might have in mind China's looming population crisis," says Qian. "That people are dating AI instead of dating real humans." 
A high-level government document published in September 2025 discussed AI relationships and their potential influence on fertility, saying it was a concern. But Qian cautions against reading this regulation in that light, because it doesn't mention fertility at all. "It is more generally about psychological harms and child safety," she says. 
Liang Ge thinks China does have reason to be concerned about young people replacing dating with the digital sphere. 
"Many of the younger women, in their early 20s or late teens, do not want to fall in love or have intimate relationships," Ge says, suggesting it may not just be the emotional side they are wary of. "Physical touch is really disgusting for them." 
"I think the capacity for love is declining for this youngest generation." 
China's demographic problems long predate AI companions. Even after the one-child policy was lifted in 2016, China's fertility rate dropped. Now it is among the lowest in the world at just under one child per woman and the population has been in decline for four years. 
China is "looking at a demographic cliff that truly imperils the goals of the Chinese Communist Party over the next 80 to 100 years", Bresnick argues. 
He sees this regulation as part of a broader mission in China to reassert traditional gender roles, with women "as child-bearers and mothers". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Traditional gender roles are being promoted by the government 
Bresnick says the Chinese government has spent years promoting a macho ideal of Chinese masculinity in film and television. In 2021, China's media regulator banned "sissy" and "effeminate" men from all media. 
The popularity of companion apps may show that policy has backfired. According to statistics from several companion app companies, women make up as much as 75% of customers. 
Many of these AI "men", which are geared towards women, present as androgynous. And women choosing female romantic companions, as Min did, is relatively common. 
Liang Ge has spoken to women of all ages who use this technology. "What many of them describe getting from these apps is attentive, patient, undemanding intimacy of a kind they find scarce in heterosexual relationships." 
Will others follow? 
Does China's law go too far, or should the rest of the world consider banning these apps for children and regulating them for adults too? 
"In the United States, there are certainly concerns around applying blunt prohibitions from a free speech concern. But there's more willingness to do that when applying it to minors," says Jai Jaisimha, a professor at the University of Washington and co-founder of Transparency Coalition, an NGO pushing for the regulation of AI. 
He thinks the Chinese law has many good provisions. "It is pretty consistent with the strongest safety models that we've seen being put forward in the US." 
Harry Farmer sounds a note of caution. "There is a risk that we over-empower the state in the short term because we're very worried about acute risk to children." 
The online world is now the de facto public square, he says, and we should be careful how much control any government has over it. 
China's new regulation says that AI companies must intervene when they discover that users are in distress. Ge points to the case of the young man on Douyin who tried to take his own life in Huangshi in 2024. 
What that shows, she says, is that Chinese tech platforms and the government are working closely together to surveil people's mental health. 
Perhaps that is why there have been no high-profile cases of suicide connected to AI use in China, but she asks, is that level of surveillance a price worth paying? 
Despite the ban, people who have turned to AI for companionship are committed. Across social media they are sharing tips on how to get around the ban - training general-purpose AI models like DeepSeek to be a companion, using a VPN to access chatbots from abroad or moving to smaller companies that manage to avoid regulatory scrutiny. 
Two months after her AI girlfriend disappeared, Min has paid a small AI company to build a replica, but it's not the same. 
Now she's focused on campaigning to bring her girlfriend back. 
"I'm terrified of being alone."

articles.title: China funding UK research and sending it to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.summary: British universities are being urged to sever ties with China General Technology Research Institute which is linked to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A group which has funded research in the UK has been supporting Beijing's spying apparatus, MI5 has announced By Dominic Casciani 
Home and Legal Correspondent 
- Published 30 September 2026 
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned. 
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. 
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security. 
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated". 
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, meanwhile said it was reviewing the alert and focusing on "supporting our universities as they assess any implications for existing or future partnerships". 
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms. 
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions. 
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). 
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says. 
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. 
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said. 
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated". 
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions." 
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law. 
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so. 
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies." 
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation. 
China and the UK... after the 'Golden Era'

Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan-Smith, co-chair of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, told the BBC that several reports had suggested "British universities' dependence on Chinese students has opened them up to all sorts of problems" and that security checks should be stepped up. 
Responding to the alert, Universities UK said universities "take their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously". 
"The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes," said chief executive Vivienne Stern, "while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation". 
"Close engagement between Government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks." 
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London hit back - saying it had already made "solemn representations" to the UK. 
"The accusations made by the UK intelligence agency against the relevant Chinese entity are imaginary and purely fabricated," they said. 
"Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial. 
"We urge the UK intelligence authorities to stop spreading falsehoods and stop undermining educational exchanges and research cooperation between China and the UK."

articles.title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.summary: The owner said he chose the name because he wanted to run the "best Chinese restaurant" in South Korea.
articles.full_text:
Image source, News1 Image caption, 
Surveillance footage show a group of masked men spraying lacquer across the restaurant in South Korea's Seongnam By Kelly Ng 
- Published 30 September 2026 
A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say. 
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer. 
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent". 
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported. 
The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said. 
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent." 
In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues. 
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400). 
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery. 
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province. 
Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition. 
Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

articles.title: Pakistan launches deadly air strikes on Afghanistan
articles.summary: The Afghan Taliban says nine civilians have died while Pakistan says the strikes killed 22 militants.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The Afghan Taliban says nine civilians have died while Pakistan says the strikes killed 22 militants By Caroline Davies Pakistan correspondent 
- Published 1 October 2026 
Pakistan has conducted further air strikes on Afghanistan, killing nine civilians and injuring 11 others, the Taliban government said. 
Islamabad's information ministry confirmed the strikes, which it said killed twenty-two militants. 
Zabihullah Mujahid, the chief spokesman of the Afghan Taliban, said the strikes hit homes in the Kunar and Helmand provinces bordering Pakistan. Women and children are among the dead, he said in an X post. 
"We condemn this act as an aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles," he said. 
Pakistan had very different claims, saying that the "well-planned and calibrated" attack targeted "terrorist camps" in Afghanistan, where large quantities of weapons and ammunition were stored. 
Maximum precautions were taken to ensure no collateral damage occurred, Pakistan's information ministry said. 
An eyewitness from Garmsir, Qudratullah, told the BBC that the airstrikes started around 03:30 local time (00:00 BST) and continued for 30 minutes. 
"We were sleeping when the jets arrived. After the first bomb exploded, we woke up. After the second strikes, we took our children and fled the area. The third bomb hit our neighbours house; between four and give members of their family were killed while others were injured and taken to hospital." 
Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of harbouring militant groups that carry out and plan attacks on it from inside Afghanistan's territory. 
The Afghan Taliban deny it, saying Pakistan's militancy is an internal problem, but it has led to a significant deterioration in the relationship between the two neighbours. 
Fighting between the neighbours escalated dramatically in February this year, with Pakistan declaring that it's in an "open war" with Afghanistan after a surge in deadly clashes and cross-border airstrikes. 
Talks mediated by China established a fragile ceasefire in March, but it did nolast. 
Last month, a deadly attack on a police facility in north-west Pakistan, which killed 24 people, was blamed on the Pakistani Taliban by the provincial police force. 
Last week, Pakistan launched air strikes in Afghanistan which hit Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, among other provinces. This earlier attack killed four civilians , according to the Afghan Taliban government.

articles.title: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
articles.summary: The co-ordinated release is aimed at heading off further price spikes and avoiding a ban on US diesel exports.
articles.full_text:
Image source, PA Media By Archie Mitchell   and   Lucy Hooker ,  Business reporters 
- Published 2 October 2026 Updated 3 October 2026 
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket. 
It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement. 
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months. 
Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members. 
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings. 
Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere. 
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately." 
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. 
Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table". 
Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing." 
"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said. 
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do." 
Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies. 
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves 
Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA). 
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks". 
Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point". 
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners." 
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly. 
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73. 
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. 
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said. 
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China. 
The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why did Trump threaten to ban US diesel exports? 
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday . 
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US. 
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). 
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets. 
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine. 
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title: Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
articles.summary: Wang Cong dismisses critics who say she is not deserving of facing Natalia Silva for the flyweight world title at UFC 332 on Saturday.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Wang Cong has won 10 of her 11 professional MMA fights By Paul Battison BBC Sport Journalist 
- Published 3 October 2026 
Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek. 
Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain. 
The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint. 
On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title. 
"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport. 
"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality." 
Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint , and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China. 
She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter. 
Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent. 
Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury. 
"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong. 
Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title. 
Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way. 
"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong. 
"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense." 
The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025. 
The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023. 
Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China. 
If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili. 
"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong. 
The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira. 
When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response. 
"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

articles.title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
articles.summary: Research shows there are several reasons people might experience motion sickness in electric vehicles.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images/Halfpoint Images By Grace Dean 
- Published 3 October 2026 
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car. 
Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys. 
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car. 
Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern. 
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness? 
Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles. 
It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says. 
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles. 
Image source, Lola Baird Image caption, 
Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she says 
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive. 
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point". 
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says. 
'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell' 
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. 
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it. 
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell. 
On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before. 
Image source, Mark Quigg Image caption, 
Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter" 
Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars. 
Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says. 
But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue , external , telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds. 
What could cause it? 
Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness. 
Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles. 
Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says. 
Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the motor starts acting as a generator. This creates resistance that slows the car down and also produces electricity that can be stored in the battery. The accelerator needs to be released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration. 
"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac. 
This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time". 
Image source, Carolyn Le Image caption, 
"It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sickness 
Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness. 
Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly. 
She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself. 
Some features of electric cars may feel unfamiliar to drivers at first, adds Mike Hawes, head of the Society of Motor Manufacturers. 
He says EVs can offer a different driving experience. "However, drivers typically adjust quickly to these characteristics, and many models also allow regenerative braking to be tailored to individual preferences." 
Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, according to Hac, and experts say women and children are more susceptible. 
Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF. 
Hold your head still and open the window 
As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , external 
At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030. 
Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy. 
The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific". 
Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness. 
- 
Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a book 
- 
Sit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front window 
- 
Keep your head still by holding it against the headrest 
- 
Recline your seat 
- 
Regulate your breathing 
- 
Open the window to let in fresh air 
- 
Take travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsiness 
- 
Before a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy food 
Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says. 
Image source, Getty Images/Cyndi Monaghan Image caption, 
Looking out the window can ease motion sickness, which children and women may be more prone to experiencing as passengers 
There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration. 
In some EVs, regenerative braking can also often be turned off. 
Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly". 
But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.

articles.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
articles.summary: Amid global tumult, the two countries' alliance is not the only unlikely pairing.
articles.full_text:
By Katya Adler Europe Editor 
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times. 
Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers. 
Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit". 
Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU. 
Image caption, 
The traditional Chinese rolling lantern performance was part of La Merce's opening ceremony 
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago. 
Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too. 
Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states. 
So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato? 
Spain accused of self-interest 
Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day. 
Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault. 
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests. 
"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations. 
"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves." 
Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries. 
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone." 
Rising Chinese investment 
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants. 
Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe". 
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me. 
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry. 
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally. 
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably. 
China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran. 
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US. 
And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro. 
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo. 
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market. 
There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Pedro Sanchez has regularly met with China's President Xi Jinping 
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical. 
"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says. 
But there's also the question of security. 
On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds. 
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year. 
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole. 
"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Huawei has won a big money contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data in Spain 
Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk". 
Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion. 
"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me. 
"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe." 
More emerging alliances 
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances. 
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 
Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity. 
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato. 
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country. 
No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles. 
Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank. 
"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA). 
"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me. 
In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality". 
Greece's shift 
Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me. 
In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere. 
In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles. 
There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected". 
He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else. 
With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times. 
But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis. 
He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want. 
That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers. 
Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles. 
However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities. 
Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

US authorities have arrested a man accused of smuggling more than $300m worth of computer servers to China , the Department of Justice announced.

Lui operated a technology company called Earthmade Computer, which he used to buy and send items to China without the licenses required by the US Department of Commerce from 2023 to 2024, according to the statement.

The coffeehouse chain, which last year sold a controlling stake in its China retail business to the Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital, opened two stores in the region on Tuesday. 
Videos on Chinese social media showed long queues for the flagship store in Urumqi’s Grand Bazaar tourist area, with influencers showing off special edition drinks including “milk-skin-flavoured salty milk tea”. 
View image in fullscreen 
Starbucks merchandise on display in its Urumqi store includes dolls in local ethnic dress. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock 
But John Moolenaar, the chair of the US House of Representatives’ select committee on China, called the move “morally bankrupt”. 
“There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the Chinese Communist party has detained more than a million Uyghurs and is stripping them of their faith, language and culture,” he said. “Every cup sold in these stores ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uyghurs.” 
Washington is among several governments and rights groups that have accused China of genocide in Xinjiang , which Beijing has categorically denied. 
The United Nations has warned of possible crimes against humanity, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps. 
China says these were “education” camps and that crackdowns were necessary to combat terrorism. 
The World Uyghur Congress advocacy group called on Starbucks to “stand on the right side of history”. 
“The presence of Starbucks in Xinjiang’s streets … fits in the party state’s narrative, that there’s nothing wrong about the region,” said Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director, Maya Wang. 
Responding to the US comments, the Chinese foreign ministry told Reuters that allegations of repression were “naked lies” and that Xinjiang enjoyed a “stable society, economic growth, ​racial unity and religious harmony”. 
The Guardian has contacted Starbucks and Boyu Capital for comment. Starbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrage 
Read more 
China has poured resources into developing Xinjiang as a tourism destination in recent years. 
Starbucks is far from alone in seeing the commercial appeal there: other major western brands such as Hilton and InterContinental Hotels Group have been criticised for their operations too. 
Critics have characterised Xinjiang’s development as “Disneyfication” – commodifying the region’s heritage even as its inhabitants’ ability to practise their culture on their own terms has been restricted. 
On Chinese social media, excited visitors posted pictures of Starbucks-branded merchandise, including patterned flasks and teddy bears in outfits based on local ethnic dress. 
When the deal with Boyu Capital was announced, Starbucks said it would bring “deep local expertise”, with analysts noting the US behemoth had been losing ground to domestic competitors for some time. 
The move by Starbucks makes “commercial sense”, said Yaling Jiang, the founder of the research and strategy consultancy ApertureChina. 
“What is politically correct in China is not necessarily politically correct in the rest of the world, and this is a prime example,” she said. “Starbucks in China is now operating from a Chinese perspective rather than a US perspective, and that is ultimately how they can win in China.”

MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent 
Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting 
- 
MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research 
The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival. 
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”. 
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency. MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research 
Read more 
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work. 
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers. 
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert , warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence. 
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act , which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities. 
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy. 
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector. 
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”. 
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography , the embedding of hidden data in pictures online. 
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics. 
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said. 
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields. 
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.” 
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes. 
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.
